what_it_does: GPU simulators used in academic research were built on a 2006 chip design, making them badly inaccurate on modern hardware. This paper reverse-engineers the inside of a modern NVIDIA Ampere GPU by running carefully crafted tiny programs that expose the chip's hidden behavior cycle by cycle. Using those findings, the authors rebuilt the simulator and cut its error rate roughly in half.
method_in_detail:
The idea. Nearly every academic paper that simulates a GPU uses a model frozen in time from 2006. Modern chips work very differently, so simulations give wrong answers and research built on them can mislead. The authors wanted to find out exactly what NVIDIA's current chips actually do inside.

How it works. Rather than guessing, they wrote hand-crafted low-level programs (in a GPU assembly language called SASS) that measure how many clock cycles individual instructions take under carefully varied conditions. By systematically changing which registers instructions read, how many programs run in parallel, and what dependency flags are set, they were able to deduce each hidden mechanism.

Key findings. First, instead of the old 'scoreboard' — a hardware circuit that watches for data conflicts between instructions — modern NVIDIA chips let the compiler itself encode timing information into control bits baked into every instruction. A 'Stall counter' tells hardware how many cycles to wait before issuing the next instruction; six 'Dependence counters' handle operations with unpredictable timing like memory loads. Second, the chip uses a 'greedy then youngest' scheduling rule: it keeps running the same stream of work until forced to switch, then picks the youngest eligible work rather than the oldest. Third, each sub-unit has a tiny, compiler-managed register cache (6 slots) that cuts costly re-reads from the main register file. Fourth, a small 16-entry prefetch buffer fetches upcoming instructions in advance, nearly matching a theoretically perfect cache at much lower cost.

The key design choice. Letting the compiler handle dependency timing rather than building dedicated scoreboard hardware saves chip area and wiring while being faster — because the compiler has more information at compile time than a scoreboard can have at runtime.

The result. The rebuilt simulator achieves 13.98% average error against real hardware on 143 benchmarks, compared to 32.22% for the old simulator — an 18-percentage-point improvement. Worst-case error drops from 543% to 62%.
